newsitem.title: USA: Tribal advocates concerned over Peru oil tests.
newsitem.headline: Tribal advocates concerned over Peru oil tests.

text.p: A London-based advocacy group Monday urged U.S. oil company Mobil Corp to stay out of Indian territory in Peru's Amazon in order to avoid harming isolated tribes.

A spokesman for the Survival International group said that Mobil's exploration activities in the Madre de Dios jungle area were putting "uncontacted" Indians at risk, as those tribes have no resistance to Western diseases.

"There is a tragic inevitability about what Mobil is doing. If they are genuinely concerned about the uncontacted Indians, they will stay out of their territory. That is the only way to ensure there will not be another disaster," Survival's Jonathan Mazower said by telephone from London.
A spokesman for the Fairfax, Va.-based Mobil said there has been no contact between its workers and the isolated Indian tribes in the Peruvian jungle.
Mobil corporate spokesman Chris Springham also denied Survival's assertion that there had been at least three encounters in the area where the oil company is carrying out seismic surveys.
"That is not true. We have not contacted the Indians at all," he said.
Springham added that, in order to deal with any eventual encounters, the company had drafted contingency plans with the support of environmental consultants and Peruvian authorities.
Their preventive measures include frequent medical examinations to test workers for diseases, he said.

Mobil did check out two reports from its workers in the area, one involving the sighting of a naked, long-haired man and another one involving a logging camp site. Neither incident resulted in contacts with Indians.

Survival International said its concerns were based on a 1985 case in which between 50 and 100 Indians in a nearby area died from pneumonia and whooping cough they caught from other oil workers and loggers.
Mobil leads a U.S.-French consortium that started conducting oil exploration work this year in two blocks covering over three million hectares in Peru's Amazonian jungle and Andean highlands.
